mandibular-distraction-osteogenesis.summary: Gradual lower-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, giving a longer, more projected jaw visible in profile.

quick.overview:
Mandibular distraction osteogenesis lengthens the lower jaw. The bone is cut, a device is attached, and the gap is slowly stretched so new bone fills it, giving a longer jaw and stronger chin projection that shows in profile.

The principle comes from Ilizarov's work on long bones, where bone forms when stretched along its axis at about 1 mm per day. The modern jaw version dates to 1992 reports, and it is best documented in children with small jaws and airway obstruction, such as Pierre Robin sequence. The literature is mostly case series and cohort reports; adults seeking it for looks are discussed in hardmaxxing circles, and no studies of purely cosmetic use were found.
quick.how: After the surgical cut there is a latency period of about a week, then the device is turned gradually, followed by a consolidation period while the new bone matures. Devices can be external or internal. The whole process runs over months and is planned and carried out by a craniofacial or maxillofacial surgeon.
quick.risks: A large review of 3,278 craniofacial cases documents complications. Reported problems include infection, hardware failure, and injury to the inferior alveolar nerve, tooth buds or the facial nerve in a minority of cases. It is a major surgery with a long treatment period.

angle.text: A surgeon cuts the lower jaw and attaches a device that slowly stretches the gap, so new bone forms and the jaw ends up longer with a more projected chin. The change is visible in profile. It is well documented in children with congenital jaw conditions, and studies of purely cosmetic use were not found.

total-maxillary-osteotomy.summary: Whole upper jaw cut and repositioned (Le Fort I) to change face length, bite and midface balance; a major established jaw operation.

quick.overview:
Total maxillary osteotomy, usually a Le Fort I operation, frees the entire upper jaw and moves it forward, up or down. The payoff people want is a changed face length, a corrected bite and better midface balance.

In medicine it treats long face (vertical maxillary excess), open bite and under-grown upper jaws, for example in cleft lip and palate. Published research is mainly surgical: studies of how the jaw keeps its blood supply, X-ray measurement of skeletal change, and peri-operative questions like anaesthesia and bleeding. In looksmaxxing it is classed as a hardmaxx procedure for changing facial structure, and the reviewed material did not measure attractiveness outcomes.
quick.how: Surgeons cut the upper jaw horizontally, free it from the skull base, reposition it and fix it in place. It is normally planned together with an orthodontist, with braces coordinated around the operation. Healing takes weeks, with months of bone remodelling.
quick.risks: General references list bleeding, swelling, infection and nausea, plus facial numbness that is usually temporary but can occasionally be permanent. It is a major operation done under general anaesthesia or deep sedation.

angle.text: The whole upper jaw is cut free and moved to a new position, changing face length, bite and midface balance. The change in facial structure is visible. The surgical literature is extensive, mostly on technique and healing rather than looks outcomes.

medpor-chin-implant.summary: Hard porous polyethylene chin implant that tissue grows into, adding lasting chin projection to balance a recessed profile.

quick.overview:
A Medpor chin implant adds chin projection to balance a recessed profile. It is a hard, slightly flexible porous polyethylene shaped to sit over the chin bone, and the added projection is visible once swelling settles.

Tissue grows into the implant's pores, which anchors it and supports blood supply. It is one of three common synthetic chin materials, alongside silicone and ePTFE. Published material is mostly technique descriptions; one plastic-surgery paper describes a modified, reshaped version for Asian patients. In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx option.
quick.how: A surgeon places a shaped implant over the chin bone through a small incision. Choice of material and shape is made with the surgeon, often compared with silicone and ePTFE. Swelling takes weeks to settle.
quick.risks: General chin-implant risks include swelling, hematoma, temporary numbness, infection, displacement and nerve damage. Because tissue grows into the pores, porous implants are harder to remove than smooth ones.

angle.text: A hard porous implant is placed over the chin bone to add projection and balance a recessed profile, with tissue growing into the pores to anchor it. The added projection is visible once healed. It is an established option, and published material is mostly technique descriptions.

eptfe-gore-tex-facial-implant.summary: Gore-Tex-type porous implant that adds volume and contour to the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose.

quick.overview:
Expanded PTFE, sold as Gore-Tex, is a flexible porous implant used to add volume to the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose. The added contour shows once healed.

It was developed in 1969 and is widely used in medicine, for example in vascular grafts and sutures. Because it is nearly inert and tissue grows into its pores, it holds in place. Cosmetic studies in the reviewed material are small and mostly older: a 1997 lip-augmentation evaluation, a rhinoplasty literature review noting both advocates and opponents of alloplast use, and an Asian nasal dorsum study.
quick.how: The material is shaped and placed in a surgical pocket. In the chin it is attached to bone with titanium screws, and tissue ingrowth provides most of the hold. It is used alongside silicone and Medpor as an implant option and is chosen with a surgeon.
quick.risks: General implant risks include swelling, infection, displacement and nerve injury. Surgeons quoted in the rhinoplasty review express hesitation about alloplast use because of historical experience with earlier nasal implants.

angle.text: A flexible Gore-Tex-type implant is placed to add volume to the chin, lips, nasolabial folds or nose, with tissue growing into the material to hold it. The added contour is visible once healed. Cosmetic studies are small and mostly older.

silicone-chin-implant.summary: Soft, removable silicone chin implant that adds projection and gives a more defined profile straight away.

quick.overview:
A silicone chin implant is a shaped piece of soft silicone placed in front of the chin bone to add projection and define the profile. The change is visible straight away, once swelling settles.

It is among the most commonly used chin implant materials, and it can be removed easily. It is one of the standard hardmaxx chin options and is often compared with Medpor, ePTFE and bone-cutting sliding genioplasty. Published material consists mostly of case reports and surgeon series on complications and facial augmentation.
quick.how: The implant sits in a pocket over the chin bone and does not bond to tissue, so its position depends on how accurately the pocket is made. Choice of size and shape is made with the surgeon.
quick.risks: Reported issues include movement, buckling, bone resorption under the implant, infection (including late infection years after surgery) and soft-tissue deformity.

angle.text: A soft silicone implant is placed over the chin bone to add projection and sharpen the profile, and it can be removed easily. The change is visible straight away. Published material is mostly case reports and surgeon series on complications.

mersiline-mesh-implant.summary: Polyester mesh named as a scaffold material for building up the chin and face; cosmetic use is niche.

quick.overview:
Mersiline mesh is named in a chin-augmentation reference as a mesh scaffold used to build up the chin or facial area for added projection or volume. The name appears to correspond to Mersilene, a polyester (Dacron) surgical mesh.

Mersilene has been used for decades in hernia repair, prolapse surgery and eyelid-lifting procedures. In looksmaxxing it is a niche hardmaxx implant option. Its facial-augmentation use is mentioned only in passing, and no cosmetic studies were found in the reviewed material.
quick.how: A woven synthetic mesh is placed as a scaffold within the tissue, the way it is used as reinforcement or suspension material elsewhere in the body. It is listed alongside other alternatives such as acellular dermal matrix and braided suture material.
quick.risks: Cosmetic risks are not documented in the reviewed sources. Studies of Mersilene mesh in other body regions report complications, for example in eyelid ptosis surgery.

angle.text: A woven polyester mesh is placed as a scaffold to build up the chin or facial area for added projection or volume. A chin-augmentation reference mentions it as an alternative implant material, and the mesh itself is established in hernia and eyelid surgery.

mustard-otoplasty.summary: Mattress-suture ear pinning that builds the antihelical fold so prominent ears sit closer to the head, without cutting cartilage.

quick.overview:
Mustardé otoplasty sets back prominent ears. Permanent mattress stitches create or deepen the antihelical fold, so the rim sits closer to the head, and the cartilage is not cut. The pinned-back ear is visible once healed.

It dates to J. C. Mustardé's 1963 paper and is commonly used for prominent ear deformity. A retrospective study of patients under 18 characterised it as a good-fast-cheap technique when assessed for quality, time and cost. Published support is mostly retrospective series and technique descriptions, and in looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx ear procedure.
quick.how: It is an open method: the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, a strip of skin is removed, and mattress sutures fold the antihelix. It is often paired with Furnas sutures for ears with a deep bowl. A surgeon performs it, usually in a single short operation.
quick.risks: Documented complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion with granulomas, scarring, and overcorrection or an unnatural contour.

angle.text: Stitches fold the ear cartilage into a natural antihelical fold, setting prominent ears closer to the head without cutting the cartilage. The pinned-back ear is visible once healed. It is a long-established technique supported mostly by retrospective series.

furnas-suture-technique.summary: Stitches from the ear bowl to the bone behind pin back ears that stick out because of a deep bowl.

quick.overview:
The Furnas technique pins back ears that stick out because of a deep or wide conchal bowl. Stitches link the back of the bowl to the tissue over the mastoid bone behind the ear, reducing the ear-to-head angle without cutting cartilage. The set-back ear is visible after healing.

Described by David Furnas in 1968, it is often paired with the Mustardé technique, which forms the antihelical fold. Published work consists of technique papers and case series, including a 2025 overview of Mustardé and Furnas otoplasty covering preparation, steps, aftercare and complications. In looksmaxxing it is classed as a hardmaxx ear option.
quick.how: A surgeon places permanent or long-lasting sutures between the conchal cartilage and the mastoid periosteum. It is typically combined with Mustardé stitches in the same operation, and swelling and dressings are part of the weeks after.
quick.risks: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, overcorrection and recurrence from suture fatigue or cartilage memory. Surgeons have described flaps to reduce extrusion and recurrence.

angle.text: Stitches anchor the ear's deep bowl to the bone-covering tissue behind it, pulling ears that stick out closer to the head, often together with Mustardé sutures. The set-back ear is visible after healing. Evidence is case series, and recurrence is a known risk.

stenstr-m-technique.summary: Ear pinning that scores the front of the antihelix cartilage so it folds back and prominent ears sit closer to the head.

quick.overview:
The Stenström technique corrects prominent ears caused by a missing antihelical fold. The front surface of the cartilage is scored or rasped so it bends backward into a natural fold, and the pinned ear is visible once healed.

It was described by Sten Stenström in 1963 and remains in use, particularly in France, with modified versions published. Reported satisfaction and correction rates come from surgical case series; controlled trials are not available.
quick.how: Abrading one side of the antihelical cartilage weakens it, so it curves toward the intact side and recreates the fold. A surgeon performs it as an ear operation, followed by weeks of healing.
quick.risks: General otoplasty complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion, asymmetry and overcorrection, and recurrence has been reported.

angle.text: The front of the ear cartilage is scored so it folds back into a natural antihelix, bringing prominent ears closer to the head. The result is visible once healed. It has been used for decades, with outcomes reported in case series.

merck-stitch-otoplasty.summary: Closed ear pinning using stitches placed through tiny stab incisions, reshaping the ear without cutting cartilage.

quick.overview:
The Merck stitch is a closed, minimally invasive ear-pinning method. Sutures are placed through small puncture incisions instead of an open cut behind the ear, reshaping the ear without cutting cartilage so it sits closer to the head.

It was published in 2013 and sits within the suture-only group of otoplasty techniques, contrasted with Mustardé's open approach and larger incision. Sources describing it are sparse and no technique-specific studies were found.
quick.how: A surgeon passes sutures through stab incisions to fold and hold the cartilage in its new shape. Because it is closed, there is no long incision behind the ear.
quick.risks: General suture-otoplasty risks include suture extrusion, hematoma, infection and recurrence. No technique-specific figures were found.

angle.text: Stitches placed through tiny stab incisions reshape the ear without a long cut or cartilage cutting, setting it closer to the head. The pinned-back ear is visible after healing. It was published in 2013, and outcome data are sparse.

incisionless-fritsch-otoplasty.summary: Ear pinning with needle-placed stitches through the skin and no incision, reshaping the antihelix and bowl.

quick.overview:
Incisionless otoplasty, associated with Fritsch, pins ears back without a skin incision. Sutures are passed through the skin by needle to shape the antihelix and set back the conchal bowl, sometimes with light scoring of the cartilage. The reshaped ear is visible after healing.

Fritsch published on the method between 1995 and 2009. Sources describe incisionless suturing as suited to mild to moderate prominence, and no technique-specific clinical studies were found.
quick.how: A surgeon places percutaneous sutures with needles to fold the antihelix, avoiding a cut behind the ear. It may be combined with superficial scoring of the cartilage.
quick.risks: General otoplasty risks apply, including suture problems, hematoma, infection and recurrence. Sources describe it as suited to milder cases, and no technique-specific figures were found.

angle.text: Needle-placed stitches through the skin shape the antihelix and ear bowl without an incision, bringing mildly to moderately prominent ears closer to the head. The result is visible after healing. Publications span 1995 to 2009, with thin outcome data.

converse-wood-smith-otoplasty.summary: Cartilage-cutting ear pinning that builds a natural-looking antihelical fold with parallel incisions and tubing sutures.

quick.overview:
The Converse–Wood-Smith technique corrects prominent ears by building a natural-looking antihelical fold. Two parallel full-thickness incisions are cut through the ear cartilage and it is shaped with tubing sutures, so the ear sits closer to the head.

Converse described a cartilage-incision method in 1955. It belongs to the cartilage-cutting group of otoplasty methods; the reviewed material offered only animal research and general descriptions.
quick.how: Full-thickness cartilage incisions let the cartilage bend into a fold held by sutures. A surgeon performs it as an open ear operation.
quick.risks: Surgeons have noted that cartilage-cutting techniques carry risks of hematoma, skin necrosis and ear deformity, which contributed to the growing use of suture-only methods.

angle.text: An older ear-pinning method that cuts parallel lines through the cartilage and shapes it with tubing sutures to build a natural-looking fold for prominent ears. The corrected shape is visible after healing. Suture-only methods have since become more common.

earlobe-reduction-repair.summary: Minor surgery that mends torn or split earlobes or shrinks oversized ones for neater, more even lobes.

quick.overview:
Earlobe repair and reduction give neater, more even lobes. Repair mends lobes torn or split by heavy earrings, trauma or gauged piercings; reduction shrinks or repositions oversized or protruding lobes. The tidier lobe is visible once healed.

Published sources are mostly surgical technique papers and small case series. One paper on cosmetic repair notes that piercing-related complications are rising with the popularity of body piercing.
quick.how: Surgeons remove scar or excess tissue and close the lobe with designs such as Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap or double-flap, chosen to avoid notching of the lobe edge. It is a minor procedure done by a plastic surgeon or similar specialist.
quick.risks: Notching at the lobe rim is the outcome the techniques aim to avoid. One L-plasty series reported no complications, and larger controlled studies were not found.

angle.text: A minor procedure that mends torn or split earlobes from heavy earrings or gauges, or shrinks oversized lobes, leaving them neater and more even. The tidier lobe is visible once healed. The literature is mostly technique papers and small case series.

ear-cartilage-molding-earwell.summary: A newborn-only splint system that reshapes soft infant ear cartilage into a normal shape without surgery.

quick.overview:
Ear molding is a non-surgical treatment for babies born with prominent (cup or protruding) ears, lop ears, Stahl's ear or constricted ears. A small molded device and adhesive guide the soft cartilage into a more typical shape over several weeks, so the child ends up with normal-shaped ears without surgery. The EarWell Infant Ear Correction System is one commercial version.

Researchers attribute the effect to maternal estrogen still circulating in the newborn, which keeps ear cartilage unusually pliable during the first weeks of life. In one single-physician review of 488 patients, only about 30 percent of congenital ear deformities were reported to self-correct. Studies are mostly case series reporting success rates from the mid-80s to mid-90s percent, and results are reported to be best when molding starts in the first one to two weeks. In looksmaxxing communities it appears as a reference point for what can be changed about ear shape and when.
quick.how: A device is attached to the baby's ear for several weeks, holding the folds of the ear (antihelix, helical rim, conchal area) in a corrected position while the cartilage sets. It is a newborn option fitted by a clinician and is not used for adults.
quick.risks: Reported complications are mostly skin irritation, pressure sores and abrasions; one tropical-climate series reported skin complications in 46 percent of infants. Some ears relapse after treatment, severe constricted ears respond less well, and results decline when treatment starts after the first weeks of life.

angle.text: A splint worn on a newborn's ear reshapes soft cartilage over several weeks, producing normal-shaped ears without surgery. It works through the pliability of infant cartilage, so studies report the best results when started in the first weeks of life. It is a newborn option and not used for adults.

corner-lip-lift.summary: Surgical skin excision at the mouth corners that raises downturned corners for a friendlier resting mouth and fuller-looking lips.

quick.overview:
A corner lip lift (also called a smile lift or commissure lift) raises downturned mouth corners. A small piece of skin is removed at or just above the corner so the corners sit higher, giving a friendlier resting mouth and, as surgeons describe it, a wider visible lip. The new mouth angle is visible once healed.

It is often performed together with an upper lip lift. Published literature is mainly surgeon-authored descriptions and case series, including a 2022 Aesthetic Surgery Journal article from authors who reported over 2,440 consecutive lip lifts, which discusses when to add a corner lift. Wikipedia notes surgeons report high satisfaction but no single lip lift technique has become standard. On looksmax.org, users discuss it for mouth width, lip fullness and smile prominence.
quick.how: Skin is excised in a lens or triangle shape above the oral commissure and the wound is closed, pulling the corner upward. Some variants also involve the muscles around the mouth. Reports describe the result as a change of a few millimetres.
quick.risks: Reported risks include visible scarring, hypertrophic scarring, asymmetry, under-correction, stiffness, numbness and distortion of the smile. A surgeon-authored review states that lip lift design is more complex than most practitioners realize, and some posters on looksmax.org say surgeons advised against the procedure for aesthetic reasons, including protecting white lip length.

angle.text: A small piece of skin is removed at the mouth corners to lift downturned commissures, giving a friendlier resting mouth and a wider, fuller-looking lip, often alongside an upper lip lift. The new mouth angle is visible once healed. Evidence is surgeon case experience, and scarring at the corner is a recognised risk.

gore-tex-lip-implant-softform.summary: A tubular Gore-Tex-type (ePTFE) implant placed in the lip for permanent added volume and fuller lips.

quick.overview:
Gore-Tex lip implants are thin strips or tubes of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) placed in the lip to add permanent volume. The fuller lip is visible after healing.

Wikipedia lists SoftForm, Advanta and UltraSoft as commercial versions, in diameters of 1.6 mm or 4.8 mm. ePTFE is a long-established implant and graft material in vascular, cardiac, hernia and facial plastic surgery. The sources reviewed describe the lip use only briefly, and no clinical studies specific to lip use were found.
quick.how: A surgeon inserts a solid or hollow ePTFE tube into the lip tissue, where it physically occupies space and increases lip volume. Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, it is a physical device rather than an injectable.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists implant movement and extrusion (breaking through the tissue) among complications of lip implants, along with bleeding, asymmetry and lumpiness.

angle.text: A thin tube of Gore-Tex-type ePTFE is placed in the lip for permanent added volume, sold under names such as Advanta, UltraSoft and SoftForm. The fuller lip is visible after healing. Sources describe it briefly, and implant movement and extrusion are listed complications.

alloderm-lip-augmentation.summary: Processed donor skin (AlloDerm) placed in the lip to add size or sharpen the lip border for fuller, crisper lips.

quick.overview:
AlloDerm lip augmentation uses processed donor dermis from cadavers, with living cells removed, to add volume to the lips. Surgeons place it in small rolls in the lip to add size, or along the lip border to sharpen the edge, according to Wikipedia. The added volume is visible once healed.

A 2000 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery is titled "Alloderm lip augmentation", but its abstract was not available, and no outcome data were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: Rolled or layered donor dermal tissue is inserted into the lip mucosa to add bulk, or into the vermilion border to define it. It is a surgical procedure done by a surgeon.
quick.risks: No specific complication data for this use were found. Wikipedia lists general lip augmentation complications such as swelling, bruising, asymmetry and lumpiness.

angle.text: Processed donor skin is placed in small rolls in the lip to add size, or along the lip border to sharpen it, giving fuller or crisper-edged lips. The added volume is visible once healed. Sources describe it briefly, with one 2000 paper title.

dermalogen-autologen.summary: Human-collagen injectable fillers that add temporary volume to the lips and soften lines.

quick.overview:
Autologen and Dermalogen are injectable dermal fillers made from human collagen, used to add volume to the lips and soften lines. Autologen is processed from the patient's own skin; Dermalogen is made from donor tissue. The filling is visible after injection.

A 2000 article on facial soft-tissue augmentation described them as physiologic and consistent with many qualities of an ideal dermal filler. A 2004 review classed them as autograft and homograft fillers respectively. Wikipedia says Autologen is absorbed quickly, so results are very temporary, and that some studies suggest Dermalogen lasts somewhat longer than standard collagen.
quick.how: Human collagen is processed and injected into the skin by a clinician, where it adds volume until the body gradually absorbs it. Results are described as short-to-moderate in duration, so use is repeated if people want to keep the look.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed describe low immune risk because the material is human-derived, with no allergy risk reported for Autologen, and results are temporary. No detailed safety trials were found.

angle.text: Injectable collagen made from the patient's own skin (Autologen) or donor tissue (Dermalogen) adds volume to the lips and softens lines. The filling is visible after injection and is gradually absorbed. Sources describe short-to-moderate persistence and low allergy risk.

mucomuscular-flap-lip-augmentation.summary: Surgical lip enlargement that moves tissue from inside the mouth into the lip for a slightly fuller, more protruding lip.

quick.overview:
Mucomuscular flap lip augmentation enlarges the lip surgically by moving tissue from inside the mouth into it. The result is slightly more bulk and a slightly more protruding lip, visible once healed.

Wikipedia describes lip augmentation by flaps, in which small strips of skin from near the lips or inside the mouth are moved to the lips, and says this adds little volume and gives only slight protrusion. No studies specific to this technique were found.
quick.how: A strip of mucosa and underlying muscle is repositioned within the lip to increase bulk. It is a surgical procedure done by a surgeon, as opposed to an injectable.
quick.risks: General lip surgery risks listed on Wikipedia include bleeding, swelling, uneven lips and lumpiness. No figures for this technique were found.

angle.text: Tissue from inside the mouth is moved into the lip to add bulk, giving a slightly fuller, more protruding lip. The change is visible once healed. The one source reviewed describes flaps generally as adding modest volume.

lip-plumper-capsaicin.summary: A chili-based lip gloss that irritates the lips into brief swelling, making them look fuller within minutes without injections.

quick.overview:
Capsaicin lip plumpers are glosses or balms containing a chili-derived irritant, sometimes with menthol, cinnamon, peppermint or ginger. They produce a tingle or burn and a short-lived swelling that makes lips look fuller within minutes. They are positioned as a needle-free alternative to filler.

Capsaicin activates heat-sensitive receptors on sensory nerves and is described as increasing blood flow and causing mild swelling, with effects reported to last from minutes to a few hours. A separate class of hydration-based plumpers uses humectants such as hyaluronic acid and does not aim to irritate. Published evidence is limited to small, mostly open-label studies of branded products.
quick.how: It is applied like a regular lip gloss or balm, often before makeup or a night out, and reapplied when the effect fades. Many products combine several active ingredients.
quick.risks: Case reports and reviews document contact urticaria and allergic contact reactions to lip cosmetics, including plumpers. Grokipedia reports that frequent use of irritant formulas may cause dryness and sensitivity.

angle.text: A chili-based gloss, sometimes with menthol or cinnamon, irritates the lips so they swell briefly and look fuller, a non-injectable option. The swelling is visible within minutes and fades in minutes to a few hours. Published studies are small and mostly open-label.
